sc01_3.text: Seriously, అంత realగా ఎలా వచ్చింది? ఈ glassesలో చిన్న screens ఉన్నాయా?
sc01_3.why: question: makes no claim; numbers and names are sourced

sc02_3.text: Cues like relative size provide depth information even when viewing with only one eye.
evidence: Monocular cues provide depth information even when viewing a scene with only one eye. Monocular cues include relative size (distant objects subtend smaller visual angles than near objects), texture gradient, occlusion, linear perspective, contrast differences, and motion parallax.

sc02_4.text: అవును, కొంచెం ఉంది. మరి రెండు కళ్లతో చూస్తే అంత ఎక్కువ ఎందుకు?
sc02_4.why: question: makes no claim; numbers and names are sourced

sc03_1.text: Your two eyes look from different but similar directions, so they see different images.
evidence: In binocular depth vision, the sensation arises from processing differences in retinal images resulting from the two eyes looking from different, but similar, directions.

sc03_3.text: Exactly. The brain combines the two views into a single picture, and that gives the perception of 3D depth.
evidence: The two images are combined in the brain to give the perception of stereopsis; when viewed, the human brain perceives the images as a single 3D view, giving the viewer the perception of 3D depth.

sc04_1.text: కానీ రెండూ ఒకే screen మీద ఉంటే, ఏది ఏ కంటికో ఎలా తెలుస్తుంది?
sc04_1.why: question: makes no claim; numbers and names are sourced

sc04_2.text: The projector puts both pictures on the same screen, each through a different filter.
evidence: To present stereoscopic images and films, two images are projected superimposed onto the same screen or displayed through different polarizing filters.

sc04_4.text: Correct. The left and right lenses have different polarizing filters, so each eye sees only its own picture.
evidence: The viewer wears low-cost eyeglasses with a polarizing filter for each eye. The left and right filters have different polarizations, so each eye receives only the image with the matching polarization.
